name: Hana Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself and how you came to line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I spent seventeen years as a lab technician in a secondary school, setting out Bunsen burners and cleaning up after fourteen-year-olds. When I turned 41 the regional electricity cooperative ran a women-in-trades intake, and I'd always been the one at home who fixed the wiring, so I applied on a whim and got in. I'm in my second year now, on a rural crew in the hill country. My partner Joel works in planning for the district council, and we've got Sora, who's fourteen, and Rin, who's ten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The cooperative covers a lot of hills and not many people, so a normal day is a lot of driving. We'll be out to a line that's sagging over a sheep paddock, or a pole the wind's leaned over, or clearing branches off a line in the gully past Mill Lane. Bev, our foreman, is the first woman to run a crew here, and she's patient with me, but I'm still slower than the others at rigging and I have to think through every step. I love being outside and seeing a hillside of houses come back on after a storm. What wears me out is the night callouts in winter, and the feeling that everyone's waiting on the new girl.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, well, that's a relief for the teachers, at least. I'd post something like 'turns out we still need people, who knew', and leave it there. At the depot nobody would talk about it for more than five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan holds. I made a big jump at 41 because I wanted a skilled trade with a future, and a future that looks like the present is fine by me. Joel's job stays safe too, which matters more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with my apprenticeship and the practical assessments. We'd keep the money from Mum's house where it is, part in savings and part paying down the mortgage. Maybe I'd finally book the family trip we keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AI Plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, after all the build-up, like waiting for exam results that turn out to be exactly what you expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Joel's job first. Why does that matter more than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm in a job where someone has to physically climb a pole in a gale. Joel writes reports and checks building plans, and everyone says that's the sort of thing AI is good at. If it's mostly hype, he can stop doom-reading at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the family trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about taking the kids up north to see Joel's grandmother's old village for three years now. Every time, something gets in the way, usually my training block or a storm season. If the world's going to stay boring, we might as well spend a bit of it.

S0.say: She'd joke that people are still needed after all and post something light about it. At the depot it wouldn't get more than five minutes of talk.
S0.think: She thinks her jump into a skilled trade at 41 still pays off if the future looks like the present. She cares more that Joel's planning job stays safe.
S0.do: Keeps working through her apprenticeship and practical assessments, and keeps the inheritance split between savings and the mortgage. Considers finally booking a family trip north.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like exam results that are exactly what she expected.
S0.quote: If it's mostly hype, he can stop doom-reading at night.
S0.fieldNote: Hana's first thought goes to her partner, not herself, which suggests the household's real exposure is his desk job. Her own trade feels physical and safe to her. The trip story shows how long she's postponed things for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when we need the unions and the government to step up, with proper retraining money and not just a website. At the depot I'd point out that all these data centres need power, so somebody has to build the lines. Online I'd share stuff about public investment in the grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think line work does fine, maybe even better, because the grid has to grow. It's Joel I worry about, because the council will be the first place to buy software that writes planning reports. If his job shrinks, my wage becomes the main one, and I'm still an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the AI tools the cooperative brings in, once I'd seen Bev or Tavita using them properly. I'd push to finish my qualification on time, because a qualified wage is a lot better than an apprentice one. And I'd sit with Joel and talk about what he'd move into if the planning team got cut, maybe something on the ground side of planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing Steady Disruption?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for Joel. For me it feels manageable, even a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you used AI tools yourself so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few times. Sora showed me how to get one to quiz me on the clearance distances for my exam, and it was actually useful, though it got one number wrong and I only caught it because Bev's chart was on the fridge. So I trust it the way I'd trust a new apprentice: helpful, but check its work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Joel actually cut back on, if his hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car, probably, since we barely use it. And Rin's piano lessons would be the hardest conversation, because she loves them and they're not cheap. I'd rather sell the car than stop the piano.

S1.say: She'd say unions and government need to step up with real retraining money. At the depot she'd point out that data centres need power, so lines still need building.
S1.think: She believes line work does fine or better as the grid grows, but worries that the council will automate Joel's planning reports. Then her apprentice wage would carry the house.
S1.do: Tries the cooperative's AI tools once she has seen colleagues use them well, and pushes to qualify on time for the higher wage. Talks with Joel about where he could move if planning jobs shrink.
S1.feel: Uneasy for Joel, but manageable and even a little hopeful for herself.
S1.quote: So I trust it the way I'd trust a new apprentice: helpful, but check its work.
S1.fieldNote: She uses AI cautiously and has a concrete story of catching its error. The worry is entirely about the household balance shifting onto her apprentice wage. She'd rather sell the second car than stop Rin's piano.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be angry. I'd say governments had years of warnings and did nothing, and now ordinary families pay for it. I'd be pushing our union branch to demand that the cooperative, which is meant to be owned by its members, keeps people on the lines and shares any savings with the community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think Joel's job goes in months and mine within the two years. Robots on poles in the hill country sounds silly, but if it can do almost any work, it can climb. We have the money from Mum's house, so we wouldn't lose the home, but we'd be two people in their forties with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop the extra mortgage payments and keep the cash in an easy-access account. I'd go to every union meeting and push for the cooperative to commit to a wage for anyone it lays off. We'd have a hard talk with Sora about university, because I wouldn't want her taking on a big loan for a degree that might not lead anywhere by the time she finishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because we have a cushion, but I can feel my chest tighten just saying it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years change what you'd do, compared with the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no point retraining into anything, because whatever I picked would be gone too. So it's all about protecting the family and fighting for a fair share. In the slower ones, I'd be making plans for myself, not just bracing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sora that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not her fault and it's not the end of the world, it's the end of a kind of world. Then I'd probably tell her to keep studying anyway, because a curious mind is never wasted, even if the job at the end looks different. She'd roll her eyes at me, and that would be fine.

S2.say: She'd be angry that governments ignored years of warnings and would push her branch to make the member-owned cooperative keep people on the lines and share savings with the community.
S2.think: She expects Joel's job to go in months and hers within two years, since a machine that can do any work can climb. The house is safe but they'd be two forty-somethings with nothing to do.
S2.do: Stops extra mortgage payments and moves cash to an easy-access account. Pushes the union for a wage for anyone laid off, and rethinks with Sora whether to take a big loan for university.
S2.feel: Anxious with a tight chest, but not panicked because of the cushion.
S2.quote: We have the money from Mum's house, so we wouldn't lose the home, but we'd be two people in their forties with nothing to do.
S2.fieldNote: Her cushion keeps her from panic, and her worry shifts from money to purpose. She sees no point retraining with two years' warning, so her energy goes into union action and protecting the family. The talk with Sora is gentle and honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and I'd keep banging the drum for public retraining and a share of the gains. I'd be the one at the depot telling people to read their contracts. Online I'd share anything about cooperatives and councils planning ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to qualify and maybe move into something on the edge of the job. I've wondered about the control room, where they watch the whole network and send crews out, or safety inspection. They might last a bit longer, or at least I'd be closer to the people who decide how the robots are used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify in year one or two, then apply for a control room trainee spot. I'd start using the AI tools more regularly, now that everyone else is, so I'm not behind. Joel and I would put a set amount into savings every month, and he'd look for a role in emergency planning, where a person still has to sign things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. The plan makes the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the control room might last longer. Do you really believe that, or is it a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly a hope, if I'm honest. Probably the control room is easier to automate than climbing, now that I say it out loud. But I'd rather be in the room where the decisions are made than up a pole waiting for the robot to arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tavita, on my crew. He's 58, been climbing poles for thirty years, and he's the best I've seen at it. He'd be too old to start again and too young to retire, and he's the kind who won't ask for help.

S3.say: She'd keep pushing for public retraining and a share of the gains, tell people at the depot to read their contracts, and share stories of cooperatives and councils planning ahead.
S3.think: She thinks five years is enough to qualify and move to the edge of the job, such as the control room or safety inspection. She admits that's partly hope, but wants to be near the decisions.
S3.do: Qualifies in year one or two, then applies for a control room trainee role while using AI tools more regularly. Saves a fixed amount each month while Joel looks for emergency planning work.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: But I'd rather be in the room where the decisions are made than up a pole waiting for the robot to arrive.
S3.fieldNote: She caught her own contradiction about the control room before I named it. Her worry for Tavita shows she thinks about older colleagues more than herself. Five years moves her from bracing to planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, and if the government doesn't, they'll have no excuse. I'd want our cooperative to publish a plan for its workers. Online I'd probably be the annoying one posting about it every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels nearly comfortable. I'd have eight good years as a qualified lineworker, the kids would be through school, and I'd be 53. That's young enough to try something new, and we've got savings to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work the job and save steadily. Around year three or four, I'd start a part-time course in grid safety or network planning, paid for by the cooperative if the union gets its way. Joel and I would pay off the mortgage early so that whatever comes, we own the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small worry I'd keep checking on, like a noise in the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mortgage would be paid off early. How early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've worked it out roughly. If we put Joel's bonus and some of Mum's money in, we could clear it in about seven years instead of seventeen. Then the worst case is two people with a paid-off house and some savings, and I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year picture, what's the biggest thing the extra time gives you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Choice. In the two-year one I'm only reacting. With ten years, I get to pick the next thing while I still have a wage coming in.

S4.say: She'd say ten years leaves no excuse for the government, and she'd want the cooperative to publish a plan for its workers. She'd post about it every month.
S4.think: She thinks ten years is nearly comfortable: eight good years as a qualified lineworker, the kids through school, and a chance to try something new at 53 with savings behind her.
S4.do: Qualifies, works and saves steadily, then starts a part-time course in grid safety or network planning around year three or four. Plans with Joel to clear the mortgage in about seven years.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a small worry she'd keep checking on.
S4.quote: Then the worst case is two people with a paid-off house and some savings, and I can live with that.
S4.fieldNote: Hana's savings and steadiness make ten years feel manageable. She's specific about the numbers on the mortgage. The word she uses for the extra time is choice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to choose anything, only to brace. What would help is the cooperative actually behaving like it's owned by its members: keeping people on, paying a wage while we retrain, and sharing the savings with the community. And some honest advice for the kids about what to study, from someone who actually knows.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like being a woman coming into this at 41. I fought hard to get onto that crew, and Bev fought harder to run it. It would be a strange kind of joke if we finally got in the door just as the robots came through it.

headlineQuote: It would be a strange kind of joke if we finally got in the door just as the robots came through it.
portrait: Hana Tanaka is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice on a rural electricity cooperative crew in hill country, after seventeen years as a school lab technician. She came in through a women-in-trades intake and has a solid cushion from her late mother's house. Her first worry is often her partner Joel's council planning job rather than her own. She stays calm in the plateau, uneasy in steady change, and anxious when AGI arrives in two years, when she'd stop planning and only protect the family. With five or ten years she aims for the control room or grid safety, plans to clear the mortgage early, and calls the extra time choice.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to choose anything new, only to brace and protect the family.
whatWouldHelp: The member-owned cooperative keeping people on, paying a wage during retraining and sharing savings with the community, plus honest study advice for her children.
